title: Does adoption spread through village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed?
summary: Research programme on the 43 Karnataka village networks of Banerjee, Chandrasekhar, Duflo and Jackson (2013; CC0 replication data, 9,126 households, 44,367 ties): can cross-sectional adoption data tell a simple contagion from a complex one, and which seeding rule stays near the best under every model the data cannot reject? Milestone 1 ports the authors’ estimation code (information model, five moments, identity weights, their 31 × 39 grid, Bayesian bootstrap). It reproduces the data (non-leader take-up 18.7% vs 18.5% published, leaders 24.7% vs 24.8%), q<sub>P</sub> > q<sub>N</sub> (98.4% of 1,000 bootstrap draws) and the counterfactual (take-up falls by 0.337 with non-adopters silent; paper 0.32), but not the published point: the minimum is q<sub>N</sub> = 0.05, q<sub>P</sub> = 0.30 for three seeds against 0.10, 0.50, which scores 11 times our minimum; q<sub>P</sub> is weakly identified (95% interval 0.15–1.0) and moves to 0.15–0.25 with two-step weights or quarterly periods. Complex contagion, identification and seeding come next.
lede: research programme: does adoption spread through real village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed? A port of Banerjee et al. (2013)'s estimation code reproduces their take-up (18.7% vs 18.5%), q<sub>P</sub> > q<sub>N</sub> (98% of bootstrap draws) and the one-third drop with non-adopters silent, but not their point estimate (0.05, 0.30 against 0.10, 0.50; q<sub>P</sub> weakly identified).
